fact_sheet.business_description: A social network allowing users to maintain identity, relationships, messages, photographs and shared content [D01]. Advertisers pay to reach targeted audiences via this large advertising platform [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Users: Social networking services for maintaining relationships/content; value derived from connections and engagement [D01].
Advertisers: Targeted audience reach; value derived from large user base and ad relevance [D01].
economics: Substantial operating leverage noted due to lack of physical store requirement for incremental ad impressions [D01].
Advertising accounts for approximately 85% of 2011 revenue; payments and other fees account for the remainder [D01].
Maintenance capex, economic compensation, and specific margin figures are not in pack [D02].
earnings_record: Q1 2012: $1.058 billion revenue, $205 million net income (vs $731 million revenue and $233 million net income in Q1 2011) [D01].
competitive_position: Moat evidence: Habitual engagement and a difficult-to-replicate social graph [D01].
Peers: Google competes for digital advertising; various social services compete for users' time [D06].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Gross IPO proceeds are not all retained corporate cash; most shares sold are secondary [D01].
No specific debt, leverage, or refinancing data provided in the pack [D02].
management_and_capital_allocation: Mark Zuckerberg expected to control approximately 55.9% of voting power post-offering [D01].
No dividend or buyback policy information provided in the pack.
price_and_valuation: Implied fully diluted equity value: ~$104 billion [D02].

yields_pct.basis: Trailing earnings yield of 0.96% derived from $1 billion 2011 net income divided by ~$104 billion fully diluted equity value [D02].

what_the_market_is_worried_about: Mobile monetization lagging behind mobile usage growth [D05].
Q1 profit declined despite revenue growth [D05].
Privacy restrictions, competition, and reliance on other platforms [D05].
Dual-class voting structure limiting minority shareholder control [D05].
deal_terms_if_any: Dual-class structure: Class A (one vote) and Class B (ten votes) [D01].
berkshire_context: Berkshire has ~$37.3 billion in cash and ~$77 billion in equity investments [D08].
missing_data: Maintenance capex, adjusted debt figures, full financial normalization, and forward earnings guidance.

understandable.evidence: As a social network subject to rapid changes in user preference and competitive pressures, it lacks the 10-20 year visibility required to be considered a durable franchise [D01], [D05], [D06].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: While the social graph and engagement represent a potential moat [D01], the platform faces significant competition from other services and advertising rivals [D06], and its pricing power is unproven in the long term.

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: The business shows recent revenue growth but experienced a profit decline in Q1 2012 [D01], [D05], which is insufficient to establish a long-term record.

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: Specific leverage, refinancing needs, and detailed ROE data are not provided in the pack [D02].

capital_intensity.evidence: The business exhibits substantial operating leverage due to a lack of physical store requirements for incremental ad impressions [D01].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: While Mark Zuckerberg maintains significant voting control [D01], the long-term track record of capital allocation and treatment of minority shareholders remains to be proven.

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: With an equity value of ~$104 billion [D02], the company is large enough to impact Berkshire's portfolio.

price_screen.evidence: A trailing earnings yield of 0.96% [D02] is significantly below the threshold required to provide a margin of safety.

gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: an unproven social platform with high engagement but significant competitive risk and an extreme valuation.

gate2.why_available: The market is valuing this business at a massive premium based on growth expectations for a platform that has yet to prove its long-term durability or pricing power [D01], [D06]. We see no reason to believe this represents a bargain, as the valuation is extreme and the business lacks the predictable, established earnings record required for our investment [D02].
evidence: Trailing earnings yield is 0.96%, far below our required threshold [D02]
Earnings declined in Q1 2012 despite revenue growth [D01]
Business lacks the 10-20 year visibility of a durable franchise [D01]
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market prices the company as a transformative, must-own growth asset despite the fundamental uncertainties regarding its future competitive position and monetization [D05].
what_must_be_true: The business would need to demonstrate a multi-decade moat and predictable pricing power
The valuation would need to align with a conservative estimate of intrinsic value
Management would need to prove capital allocation skill over a full market cycle

key_assumptions: Assumed maintenance capex is zero due to lack of data [D02]
Future growth rates are highly speculative [D01]
intrinsic_value_range.discount_rate_used: long bond rate not provided in pack [D02]

gate3.price_vs_value: price is 104x trailing earnings; margin of safety does not exist [D02]
gate3.alternatives: bonds / T-bills / existing holdings / Berkshire buyback — Berkshire cash holdings of $37.3B [D08] are safer and offer higher certainty than an unproven asset at 104x earnings
gate3.downside_case: permanent loss of capital possible if the business fails to maintain competitive advantage or monetize mobile platform [D05]
flagged_assumptions: Maintenance capex is assumed to be zero due to missing data [D02]
Long-term government bond rate is missing from the pack [D02]

gate4.role_description: We are a permanent, passive holder of marketable securities. We look for businesses with durable competitive advantages and consistent earnings records, which we hold indefinitely [D01], [D06].
value_realisation_path: value is realised through the compounding of owner earnings over long periods [D01]
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: For marketable securities in the 2000-2015 era, our edge is patience and the deployment of our permanent capital into wonderful businesses at fair prices; this opportunity fails to meet our standards for inclusion in the portfolio.

kill_criteria: pricing power lost to more effective targeted advertising competitors
user engagement declines as demographics shift or social fatigue sets in
inability to effectively monetize the transition from desktop to mobile platforms
regulator restricts data usage or privacy practices, impairing the advertising business model
gate5.berkshire_constraints: Berkshire maintains a cash floor of at least $30 billion to ensure financial strength [D08].
gate5.opportunity_cost: Capital is better deployed into existing, predictable high-return businesses or held in cash given our $37.3 billion balance [D08].
gate5.decider_reason: This investment falls into the 'too hard' category due to the lack of a 10-20 year track record and the inability to assess the durability of the competitive advantage.
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: We risk permanent loss of capital because the company lacks a proven long-term earnings record and currently trades at a valuation that assumes future growth that may never materialize.

valuation.downside_case: Permanent loss of capital if the competitive position erodes or monetization fails.

drivers.driver: The company trades at an earnings yield of 0.96%, which is fundamentally unattractive compared to the safety of our cash equivalents [D02].
We require a predictable 10-20 year track record of durable earnings to evaluate a franchise, which this business currently lacks [D01].
The valuation implies a massive growth trajectory that we cannot verify, moving the idea firmly into our 'too hard' pile [D01], [D02].
Advertising revenue, which comprises 85% of the business, faces significant competitive and platform risks that make its long-term pricing power uncertain [D01], [D06].

kill_criteria: pricing power lost to more effective targeted advertising competitors
user engagement declines as demographics shift or social fatigue sets in
inability to effectively monetize the transition from desktop to mobile platforms
regulator restricts data usage or privacy practices, impairing the advertising business model
final.what_would_change_our_mind: A demonstrated multi-decade track record of consistent, high-return earnings and a valuation that provides a substantial margin of safety.
final.memo:
Charlie and I have looked at the business of Facebook, a platform that connects millions through shared content and advertising [D01]. While the company has achieved significant scale in its user base, we find ourselves unable to gauge the durability of its competitive position over the next several decades [D01]. A business that we invest in must possess a clear, long-term moat, and the rapid evolution of social networking leaves us with too many unanswered questions [D01], [D06].

Our evaluation of the economics is hampered by the lack of a sufficient record [D01]. While the business model benefits from operating leverage, we have seen recent profit declines in the face of rising competition [D01], [D05]. We simply do not know if the platform will maintain its pricing power or if the current engagement levels are a permanent feature of the landscape [D01], [D06].

Regarding capital allocation, we are asked to pay a premium that implies a degree of certainty we do not possess [D02]. At an initial earnings yield of 0.96%, the price offers no margin of safety for the investor [D02]. We have $37.3 billion in cash and equivalent alternatives that offer far more certainty than this speculative valuation [D08]. In the world of investing, it is not necessary to swing at every pitch; we prefer to wait for the one that is squarely in our circle of competence [D02].
